name: Part 1 — Interview
tagline: Four minutes, twelve questions, no time to think
blurb: Part 1 is not a warm-up in the sense most candidates assume. It is a rapid sample of your everyday language, taken across a dozen short answers, and it is where the examiner forms the working hypothesis that Parts 2 and 3 either confirm or overturn.

facts: 4 to 5 minutes, immediately after identity checks.
Three frames. The first is always home, work or study. The next two are drawn from a fixed list of everyday topics.
Roughly ten to twelve questions. That is around twenty seconds of speaking time per answer.
Fixed. The examiner reads from a booklet and may not rephrase, explain or expand a question. If you do not understand, they can repeat it once, verbatim.
Expected. The examiner will cut you off to stay on schedule. Being stopped is a timing event, not a judgement.
brief.what: Across twelve short answers the examiner is sampling breadth. Because the answers are short and numerous, repetition is far more audible here than anywhere else in the test: six answers beginning I think, four instances of very interesting, and the Lexical Resource impression is set before Part 2 begins. Part 1 rewards the candidate who can say ordinary things in a varied, natural way, not the candidate with the largest vocabulary.
myths: Past about thirty seconds the examiner has to interrupt, and an over-long Part 1 answer is the commonest signal of a rehearsed script. Two to four sentences is the band-appropriate length.
“I must use idioms to show range.”
Idiom forced into a question about your morning routine reads as inappropriate register, which is explicitly penalised under Lexical Resource. Save idiom for where it fits.
Nothing is fact-checked. But invented answers are harder to make specific, and specificity is what makes an answer sound unrehearsed. Borrow from real life and adjust.
“If I don't know, I should say so and stop.”
Saying you have no experience of something is fine; stopping there is not. The recovery move is the hypothetical bridge, below.

tactics.name: Answer in the first clause
tactics.why: The examiner is rating coherence from the opening words. A preamble delays the answer and eats the twenty seconds you have.
tactics.do: Put the answer itself in clause one, then justify. Do you like cooking? → Not really, if I'm honest — I can manage the basics but I find it a chore rather than a pleasure.
tactics.dont: Well, that's an interesting question. Cooking is something that many people in my country…

band.b7: States it with a qualifier — not really, up to a point, it depends on the week.
band.b8: States it, then quietly recasts the question — it depends what you mean by cooking; assembling things, yes, actual cooking, no.

tactics.name: The three-beat engine
tactics.why: Under pressure candidates either stop after one clause or ramble. A fixed three-beat shape removes the decision.
tactics.do: Answer → Reason → Anchor. The anchor is a concrete particular: a name, a number, a time of day, a brand. Do you use headphones? — Constantly. I commute about forty minutes each way, and without them the noise gets to me. I've had the same pair of cheap wired ones for three years now.
tactics.dont: Answer → Reason → second reason → third reason. Additional reasons are not development; they are a list.

band.b6: Answer and reason, twenty to thirty words.
band.b7: Answer, reason and one concrete anchor.
band.b8: The anchor carries an attitude as well as a fact — the same cheap wired pair for three years, which tells you everything about my priorities.

tactics.name: Never restate the question
tactics.why: Restating is the most reliable tell of a memorised answer, and it wastes the only currency you have here, which is time.
tactics.do: Go straight in. If you need a half-second, use a genuine filler that native speakers use — Oh, definitely. Hmm, not often.
tactics.dont: Whether I often go to parks — well, going to parks is something that…

band.b7: Uses natural short fillers rather than silence.
band.b8: Uses the filler to carry attitude — a drawn-out weeell… that signals ambivalence before the words do.

tactics.name: Rotate your openers
tactics.why: Twelve answers means twelve openings. The examiner hears the pattern even if you do not.
tactics.do: Keep four or five in circulation: Honestly… / Not especially… / I'd say so, yes… / It varies, actually… / Funnily enough…

band.b7: Openers vary in function as well as wording — conceding, affirming, qualifying.
band.b8: Openers are chosen for the individual question rather than drawn from a rotation.

tactics.name: The hypothetical bridge
tactics.why: Part 1 topics are drawn from a fixed list, so you will be asked about something you have never done. Silence there costs more than the missing experience does.
tactics.do: Have you ever collected anything? — I haven't, no. I've never had the patience for it. Though if I ever did take it up, it would probably be something small and cheap, like matchboxes or old stamps. The second conditional here is free Grammatical Range.

band.b6: Says no, then offers a related fact.
band.b7: Says no, then pivots to a hypothetical with would.
band.b8: Says no, pivots, and explains what the absence says about them.

tactics.name: Attitude over information
tactics.why: Part 1 questions look factual and are not. What is the weather like where you live? is an invitation to have a view about the weather.
tactics.do: Report the fact in half a clause, then spend the rest on how you feel about it. Humid for about eight months of the year — which I've never adjusted to, despite growing up here.

band.b6: Fact plus a simple evaluation — it's very hot, I don't like it.
band.b7: Fact plus an evaluation with nuance — which I've never adjusted to.
band.b8: Fact plus evaluation plus a complicating detail — despite growing up here.

lang.intro: Part 1 language is not advanced language. It is flexible everyday language: frequency, preference, degree and hedging. These are the four functions that come up in almost every Part 1 answer, and the candidate who can vary them stops sounding like a textbook within three questions.

items: Natural spoken alternative to rarely. Note the stress falls on hard, not on ever.
Occasionally, with a sense of pleasant irregularity. and reduces to /ən/.
a couple of times a week
couple of collapses to /ˈkʌplə/ in speech. Saying it in full sounds bookish.
Every single time without fail, usually said with faint self-mockery. I check the news religiously, which is probably unhealthy.
Intermittently over a long period. I've been learning the guitar on and off for years.
The most useful polite negative in Part 1. Softer than no and it buys you a clause.
Marks sincerity. Overused it becomes a verbal tic, so once per interview.
Emphatic refusal with humour. I have absolutely no interest in football, which makes me a difficult guest.
Downgrades a noun in a very British way. It's a bit of a chore. He's a bit of a perfectionist.
Comparative with force. It's nothing like as crowded as it used to be.
= I would rather. Followed by a bare infinitive. I'd sooner walk than sit in traffic.
Signals a weak preference honestly, which sounds far more credible than a strong one.
Acceptable only if the next clause says what it depends on. Alone it is an empty answer.
Introduces a concession about something you have just criticised.
Genuine tentativeness. Reduces to /aɪ spəʊz/ in connected speech.
Closes an incomplete list the way native speakers do. Examiners hear this as fluency, not as imprecision.
Approximates a number. Twenty minutes or so.
Approximates with a margin. Three years, give or take.
Softens an adjective. Fine in Part 1; avoid in Part 3 where precision is being assessed.

phon.intro: Part 1 answers are short, so there is nowhere to hide a flat delivery. Three features do almost all the work here.

items.what: English stresses the words that carry meaning — nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs — and reduces the rest. Vietnamese is syllable-timed, so the default transfer is equal weight on every word, which the descriptors register as limited control of phonological features.
items.drill: I HARDly EVer GO, to be HONest // it's a BIT of a TREK from my PLACE
items.note: Say it first tapping the desk on the capitals only. The unstressed words should feel rushed and almost swallowed. That compression is the target, not clarity on every syllable.

items.what: to → /tə/, and → /ən/, of → /əv/ or /ə/, for → /fə/, I would → I'd. This single change does more for perceived naturalness than any amount of new vocabulary.
items.drill: I'd SOONer walk‿than SIT in a CAR for‿an HOUR → /aɪd ˈsuːnə wɔːk ðən sɪt ɪn ə kɑː fərən ˈaʊə/
items.note: If for an hour takes as long to say as sit in a car, the weak forms are not happening yet.

items.what: A rise at the end of a statement reads in English as uncertainty or as an unfinished thought. Many candidates rise on every clause, and the examiner hears hesitancy that the candidate does not feel.
items.drill: Not parTICularly ↘ // I USED to, when I was YOUNGer ↘ // but these DAYS ↗ I'd rather READ ↘
items.note: Rise only on the non-final clause to signal that more is coming. Fall to close. Record yourself and listen to the ends of sentences alone.

drills.name: Rapid fire — twelve answers, no preparation
drills.set: Twelve Part 1 questions in sequence, thirty seconds each, no thinking time between them.
drills.aim: Trains the three-beat engine until it stops requiring a decision. Do not aim for brilliance; aim for twelve answers that all land between twenty and thirty-five seconds.

drills.name: Opener rotation
drills.set: Eight questions. Rule: no opening formula may be repeated.
drills.aim: Forces the variation the examiner is listening for. Listen back and write down each opener you used.

drills.name: Hypothetical bridge
drills.set: Six questions about things you have never done or do not like.
drills.aim: Every answer must contain a second conditional. Free marks under Grammatical Range.

check: fc
Each answer ran between two and four sentences — neither a bare reply nor a speech.
fc
I answered in the first clause rather than restating the question.
fc
No opening formula appeared more than twice across the set.
lr
Each answer contained one concrete anchor: a name, a number, a time, a place.
lr
I varied frequency and degree language rather than repeating often and very.
lr
Register stayed conversational — no idiom forced into an everyday topic.
gr
At least one answer used a second conditional or a hypothetical.
gr
Tense choice matched the question — present for habit, past for childhood.
pr
Unstressed words were audibly compressed, not given equal weight.
pr
Statements fell at the end; rises were reserved for non-final clauses.

strategies.intro: Part 1 questions come in six recognisable shapes, and each shape has a development route that works and several that do not. Recognising the shape in the first two seconds is what buys you the remaining twenty-eight. The six below account for virtually every question in the compulsory frames and the topic frames alike.

groups.cue: Opens with Do you like / enjoy / prefer and names one thing.
moves: Give the verdict in the first two words. Not especially. Very much, yes.
The reason should be about you, not about the thing. I find it a chore beats cooking is difficult.
The anchor is a particular: what you cook, how often, the last time.

ex.a: Not especially, if I'm honest. I can manage the basics, but I've never found it relaxing the way other people seem to — it's a chore that happens to produce dinner. The most ambitious thing I've made this month is fried rice, and even that was mostly leftovers.

groups.trap: Answering about the topic in general instead of about yourself. The examiner is sampling your everyday language, not your knowledge of cuisine.

groups.cue: Asks for a rate, not a judgement.
groups.shape: Rate → Condition → Contrast with the past
moves: Never answer with a bare number. Twice a week is a complete fact and an incomplete answer.
Add the condition that governs the rate: depending on how busy work is.
A past contrast is free grammar — used to, would, past simple.

ex.q: How often do you go to parks?
ex.a: Hardly ever now, which I'm slightly ashamed of. Maybe once a month, and usually only because somebody else suggests it. I used to go almost daily when I lived closer to one — the difference is purely how far I have to walk.

groups.trap: Saying sometimes or usually and stopping. These are the two vaguest words available and they carry no lexical credit.

groups.type: Childhood — Did you… when you were a child?
groups.cue: Past reference, almost always paired with a present-tense follow-up.
moves: Answer in the past simple, then produce one specific memory, not a general description of childhood.
Close by linking to the present. The examiner's next question is usually about now, and pre-empting it reads as coherence.
used to and would both belong here. Would for repeated actions is the more sophisticated choice.

ex.q: Did you go for long walks when you were a child?
ex.a: Constantly — my grandmother didn't drive, so everything was on foot. We'd walk forty minutes to the market every Sunday and she'd name every plant on the way, which I found unbearably slow at eight and miss enormously now.

groups.trap: Describing childhood in the abstract. One remembered Sunday outscores three sentences about what children generally did.

groups.type: Comparison — Do you prefer A or B?
groups.shape: Lean → What each is good for → Which situation decides it
moves: Lean one way, do not refuse to choose. Both are good is a non-answer.
Name what each option is actually for. That is the reasoning the question is inviting.
Close on the deciding condition, which delivers a subordinate clause for free.

ex.q: Do you prefer shopping online or in shops?
ex.a: Online, for anything I've bought before. It takes four minutes and I know exactly what's arriving. But for clothes I'd sooner go in person — sizing is a lottery otherwise, and I've returned enough parcels to have learned that the hard way.

groups.trap: Dividing the answer exactly 50/50. Balance here reads as indecision; a lean with a reasoned exception reads as control.

groups.type: Your country — Do people in your country…?
groups.cue: Asks you to generalise about a population.
groups.shape: Hedged generalisation → Split the population → Your own position
moves: Hedge the generalisation properly: by and large, as a rule, more often than not.
Split by age, region or generation. This is the single most reliable development move for this type.
End by placing yourself inside or outside the pattern.

ex.q: Are street markets common in your country?
ex.a: Very much so, though it depends who you ask. In smaller towns they're still where most people buy food. In Hanoi the younger crowd has drifted towards supermarkets — more convenient, less haggling. I'm somewhere in between: markets for vegetables, supermarket for everything else.

groups.trap: Speaking for eighty million people with no hedge. It sounds overconfident, and it wastes the easiest categorisation opportunity in Part 1.

groups.type: Hypothetical — Would you like to…? / Would you ever…?
groups.cue: Uses would. Asks about something you have not done.
groups.shape: Would-answer → Conditional reason → What would have to change
moves: Match the modal. If the question uses would, the answer uses would.
Give the reason as a conditional, which is the grammar the question is fishing for.
What would have to change is a ready-made third sentence that always works.

ex.q: Would you like to travel to space?
ex.a: Honestly, no — I'd be terrified, and I'm not convinced I'd see anything I couldn't see in a photograph. If it were a two-hour trip with a guaranteed return, I might reconsider, but at present the risk-to-view ratio is all wrong.

groups.trap: Answering in the present simple. I don't like space answers a different question and loses the conditional.

extra.title: The it depends tactic, done properly
extra.html:
It depends is the most overused phrase in Part 1 and one of the most useful, and the difference between the two versions is a single clause.

The version that costs marks. Do you like watching films? — It depends. Sometimes yes, sometimes no. Nothing has been said. The examiner has no language to rate and no content to follow up.

The version that earns them. It depends must be followed immediately by what it depends on, and then by both cases, briefly.

Do you like watching films? — It depends entirely on who I'm with. On my own I'll happily sit through something slow and difficult. With friends it has to be something nobody has to concentrate on, or the conversation dies and everyone checks their phone.

Three things happen in those two sentences: a governing variable is named, two contrasting cases are given, and each case carries a concrete detail. That is a complete Part 1 answer, and the structure transfers to any question in any topic.

When not to use it. If the honest answer is a clear yes or no, saying it depends is evasion and sounds like it. Reserve it for questions where the variable is real.
